messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun, a 29-year-old painter from a South Asian background, found himself ensnared in a web of anxiety and fear following a traumatic mugging last year. The incident had left an indelible mark on him. He vividly recalled the evening when he was walking home from a late job, paintbrushes still tucked under his arm, when a group of men confronted him. He remembered the rush of adrenaline, the fear coursing through his veins as they demanded his wallet and phone. The ordeal lasted mere minutes, but it felt like an eternity, and he would wake up in a cold sweat, haunted by nightmares of the event—dreams where he relived the moment again and again, the panic rising in his chest as he struggled to break free. Each time he awoke, he felt a surge of irritability, an angry outburst bubbling just beneath the surface. It was as if he had become a stranger to himself, his body always on high alert, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. 

The physical locations where the mugging had occurred became charged with anxiety. Simply passing by those streets triggered a rush of intrusive memories, causing his heart to race and his palms to sweat. These moments magnified the tense state his body had adopted; he felt as if he were perpetually ready to react to danger, a sensation that transformed his daily life into a battleground. The world outside was a constant reminder of his trauma, and each spatial trigger intensified his belief that he could no longer trust the people around him. He had come to mistrust everyone, convinced that anyone could become a threat, and this growing isolation made him feel more detached from those he loved. 

As he grappled with these feelings, Arjun found it difficult to piece together the memory of the mugging. He often felt as though he was only recalling fragments of the experience, the gaps gnawing at him and fueling his guilt. He would sit in his studio, attempting to deliberate on the event, but the harder he tried to access the painful recollections, the more elusive they became. This incomplete picture of the traumatic event compounded his feelings of guilt; he often questioned why he hadn’t fought back or run faster, which only deepened his sense of inadequacy. The memories, though fragmented, remained potent triggers—each recall would send him spiraling back into that moment of vulnerability, enhancing his sense of danger and leading him to believe that he was incapable of relying on anyone, not even himself.

Arjun's negative appraisals shaped his perception of the world, creating a vicious cycle. His mistrust of people steered him towards isolation, which only fortified his belief that he couldn’t rely on others. As he withdrew from social interactions, he would find himself alone in his thoughts, the memories of the mugging replaying in his mind, reinforcing his feelings of vulnerability. This constant reflection contributed to his irritability and made him more sensitive to perceived slights from others, aggravating his readiness to react defensively. Each day became a struggle as he navigated through the layers of his trauma, caught in an ever-tightening loop of anxiety and avoidance.

When Arjun finally sought help, he felt a glimmer of hope mixed with the fear of confronting his trauma. He harbored a deep-seated worry that delving into his memories would only serve to amplify his feelings of guilt and mistrust, but he knew he could not continue living in this state of hypervigilance. He longed to reclaim the joy he once found in painting, to reconnect with his wife and friends without the shadow of his trauma looming overhead. With each session, he hoped to find a way to unravel the knots of his experience, to understand the connection between the past and present, and to ultimately heal from the scars that had come to define his daily existence.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where triggers lead to a sense of threat.
The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where triggers lead to memory.
The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where negative appraisals lead to a sense of threat.
The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where negative appraisals lead to triggers.
The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory leads to a sense of threat.
The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory leads to negative appraisals.
The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory leads to triggers.
The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where threat leads to triggers.
